name: Authoritarianism
summary: Authoritarianism favours strong, concentrated central power over political plurality, using control of the armed forces, restricted civil liberties and managed or absent elections to preserve order and the existing regime. Adherents stress obedience, security and conformity over individual freedom and competitive politics. It is a form of rule rather than an economic programme, so it takes few positions on economics or social policy.
scope: The general political outlook behind authoritarian regimes as defined by Juan Linz and described in encyclopedic summaries, supplemented by Hobbes's case for indivisible sovereign power and Altemeyer's account of authoritarian attitudes. It excludes totalitarian movements with elaborate guiding ideologies (see totalitarianism), and specific variants such as authoritarian conservatism or authoritarian capitalism. Because the label covers regimes of left, right, religious and military kinds, most economic, religious and foreign-policy answers are neutral or low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Juan José Linz
keyFigures.role: Political scientist whose typology defined authoritarian regimes.

keyFigures.name: Thomas Hobbes
keyFigures.role: Philosopher who argued for an indivisible, unaccountable sovereign.

keyFigures.name: Bob Altemeyer
keyFigures.role: Psychologist who defined right-wing authoritarian attitudes.

sources.title: Authoritarianism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Definition, concentrated power, limited civil liberties, managed elections, regime tools (Przeworski, Svolik, Tushnet, Norris and Inglehart).

sources.title: Juan José Linz
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Linz's four qualities of authoritarian regimes: limited pluralism, appeals to emotion for legitimacy, minimal mobilization, ill-defined executive powers.

sources.title: Leviathan, Chapter XVIII (Of the Rights of Sovereigns by Institution)
sources.author: Thomas Hobbes, via Project Gutenberg
sources.usedFor: Classical case for unaccountable, indivisible sovereign power: subjects cannot depose or punish the sovereign, who judges which doctrines are taught.

sources.title: Right-wing authoritarianism
sources.author: Wikipedia (summarizing Bob Altemeyer)
sources.usedFor: Authoritarian submission, aggression and conventionalism, and the attitudes to punishment, minorities and tradition that follow.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Authoritarian regimes run both generous welfare states and minimal ones; the sources define the system by control of power, not by health policy.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage policy is not part of the definition; Przeworski's point is only that prosperity helps regimes last, and regimes differ on how to get it.

public-ownership.rationale: Ownership of utilities varies across authoritarian states; the sources treat the economy as a means of regime stability, not a doctrine.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Authoritarian rulers regulate or favor business by their own interest; the sources record no consistent stance.

cut-welfare.rationale: Regimes both expand welfare to buy loyalty and cut it; no defining position.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Wikipedia lists social controls and repression of challengers as central to authoritarian rule, and Altemeyer's authoritarian aggression targets perceived threats to order.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Authoritarian rulers restrict speech, but they do so to silence opposition, not to protect minorities; adherents are split on this specific aim.

strong-leader.rationale: Linz's executive with ill-defined, expandable powers and the Wikipedia description of concentrated power under one person make a strong leader above gridlock central.

state-harmful.rationale: Hobbes grounds the whole case on the sovereign, without whom life is war; authoritarians hold strong central authority is necessary.

empower-police-military.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.

reviewHistory.rationale: Rule is maintained by control of armed forces and repression of challengers, and Altemeyer links the outlook to submission to and support for force against threats.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

rehabilitation.rationale: Altemeyer reports high authoritarian-aggression followers favor harsh punishment, including corporal punishment, over leniency.

traditional-family.rationale: Conventionalism, adherence to traditional social norms, is one of Altemeyer's three clusters.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Altemeyer lists hostility toward homosexuals and nonconformists as a result of authoritarian conventionalism; not every regime takes this line.

more-religion-public.rationale: The sources show religion backing authoritarian rule in Iran and the Taliban, yet many authoritarian regimes are secular, so adherents split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Conventionalism asks everyone to follow traditional norms, which in practice means preserving established national culture.

gradual-change.rationale: Authoritarianism preserves the status quo, but repressive rulers also impose rapid change from above; adherents are split.

free-trade.rationale: Authoritarian economic policy ranges from open trade to autarky; no defining position.

open-borders.rationale: Hostility to outgroups and emphasis on order and security make open borders contrary to the outlook.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Authoritarians could favour state command but the ideology takes no position; adherents split.

revolution-justified.rationale: Hobbes holds that subjects cannot change the form of government without injustice, and authoritarian rule aims to preserve the existing order, though Linz's regimes include some that came to power by revolution or coup.

central-planning.rationale: Some authoritarian regimes plan centrally and others protect markets; no defining position.

socialized-markets.rationale: The economic system is not defining for authoritarianism.

land-value-tax.rationale: A technical tax question the sources never touch.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Trade policy varies widely among authoritarian states.

death-penalty.rationale: Altemeyer reports support for harsh punishment including the death penalty among authoritarian followers.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Altemeyer's conventionalism expects everyone to follow traditional norms and is uncomfortable with deviation, the opposite of encouraging eccentricity.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Przeworski's view that regimes rest on lies, fear and prosperity, and Wikipedia's account of rule justified by development, support trading political freedom for growth.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Foreign policy details vary by regime and are not defining.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Elections for heads of state in authoritarian regimes tend to be managed; the doctrine is split between direct plebiscites and appointment.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Hobbes lets the sovereign set property; adherents could agree or not on common-good wording, so split.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Some authoritarian regimes curb the church and others ally with it, as Linz's Spain and Iran show.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Linz allows rule by a leader, party or military; whether the head stands above parties is not defining.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Hobbes holds the sovereign cannot be accused or punished by subjects and may commit iniquity but not injustice, and Wikipedia notes authoritarian constitutions generally do not limit the executive.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Hobbes argues sovereignty is indivisible and a divided power invites war; authoritarianism concentrates power.

leader-cult.rationale: Wikipedia lists indoctrination and loyalty building around a single leader as regime tools, though Linz says authoritarian mobilization is limited, so not forceful.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist debate outside authoritarianism as a general ideology.

land-redistribution.rationale: Land policy varies by regime and is not defining.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Some regimes assert such claims, but the ideology is silent; adherents split.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Only religious-authority regimes such as Iran take this line; authoritarianism broadly does not.

women-must-cover.rationale: Only theocratic regimes such as the Taliban impose this; secular authoritarians do not.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-national unions are a feature of specific nationalisms, not of authoritarianism in general.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: A Marxist theory that authoritarianism does not endorse or reject.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailout policy is economic and varies between authoritarian states.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Authoritarian rulers resist limits by courts, but not by deferring to a majority; the statement does not fit and adherents split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarky is a feature of some regimes only.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Hereditary rule appears in some authoritarian regimes and not others.

patriotic-education.rationale: Wikipedia lists socialization and indoctrination to build loyalty as regime tools.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Some regimes pursue neo-imperial influence and others do not; the sources give no general position.

delink-world-market.rationale: Delinking is a dependency-theory proposal that the sources do not connect to authoritarian rule.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Wikipedia says authoritarian constitutions generally do not limit executive power, so an entrenched rights document that binds government runs against the outlook.

elective-rulers.rationale: Wikipedia says leaders can be self-appointed and hold office indefinitely, without free choice among competitors.

minority-veto.rationale: Hobbes holds that once the majority declares for a sovereign the dissenting minority must submit.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Hobbes holds that subjects may not depose or punish the sovereign even if he does wrong, which is the authoritarian view of obedience, but Hobbes stands in for a regime type rather than a movement.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Linz describes constrained legislatures and ill-defined executive power, with the executive dominant over parliament.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Linz defines authoritarian regimes by minimal political mobilization, so a depoliticized, withdrawn citizenry suits the regime.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Wikipedia names lies, fear and prosperity as sources of stability; the cultural-hegemony framing is a critical theory authoritarians would not adopt.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: A world-systems claim outside what the sources cover.

party-own-road.rationale: A communist-movement question outside general authoritarianism.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Self-reliance is a policy of some regimes and not of others.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentism is a feature of some regimes, but Linz notes no elaborate ideology for authoritarian regimes in general.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Linz distinguishes authoritarian from totalitarian regimes but does not ask for joint condemnation; adherents split.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A historical dispute not tied to authoritarianism.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Authoritarian rulers commonly defend non-liberal forms as suited to their societies, as with Tushnet's authoritarian constitutionalism; moderately stated.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Wikipedia describes rule tied to the military and control of armed forces as a basis of regimes, and Linz's authoritarian cases include military regimes.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Rule rests on leaders removable only outside free choice by citizens, so binding and removable leaders contradict it.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Linz notes constrained legislatures, so a legislative veto over spending is contrary to the model.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Supporting foreign insurgents is a foreign-policy tool of some regimes, not a defining doctrine.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Bloc discipline is characteristic of particular alliances (for example Soviet-era), not of authoritarianism in general.

job-guarantee.rationale: Employment guarantees appear in communist states but not generally, so the sources give no stance.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Hobbes holds subjects authored the sovereign's acts and owe obedience, and Altemeyer describes respect for authority as a moral duty.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Altemeyer finds hostility to scapegoated outgroups, but that is a follower tendency, not a defining doctrine; split.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Wikipedia notes control of information and indoctrination as regime tools, and rulers resist open access.

informal-organisation.rationale: Linz's regimes limit and suppress autonomous anti-regime organization, so informal political groups are opposed.

religious-nation.rationale: Some regimes (Iran, Taliban) rest on religion and others are secular.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: A communist-doctrine detail that the sources do not connect to authoritarianism generally.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: A Marxist historical claim, which authoritarian regimes of left and right see differently.

socialized-care.rationale: Public childcare policy differs by regime and is not covered by the sources.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language purism belongs to specific nationalisms, not to authoritarianism in general.

majority-settlement.rationale: Settlement of majorities in minority regions is a policy of some regimes, not a general position.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Altemeyer's conventionalism expects everyone to conform to traditional norms, which in practice means immigrants assimilating.

ban-interest.rationale: Only religious regimes take this line.

bound-labor.rationale: A feudal arrangement not tied to authoritarianism in the sources.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Hobbes gives the sovereign the right to decide which doctrines may be taught and published, and Altemeyer notes conventionalism and enforcement of norms.

clerical-rule.rationale: Wikipedia cites Iran and the Taliban as clerical authoritarian rule, but most authoritarian regimes are secular, so adherents split.

collective-farming.rationale: Collectivized farming appears in communist authoritarian states but not in military or capitalist ones.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Social-Darwinist views appear in some strands but the sources do not make competition a defining idea.

conscription.rationale: Hobbes grants the sovereign the rights of war and peace and of raising forces, and notes subjects need not fight only by voluntary undertaking, so adherents accept conscription broadly.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Wikipedia describes leaders as self-appointed and removable only outside free choice, so legitimacy does not rest on consent in the liberal sense; Hobbes bases it on covenant instead, hence not forceful.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Some authoritarian regimes use state-recognized bodies, as Linz notes limited pluralism; not a defining stance.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Altemeyer's authoritarian submission treats loyalty to legitimate authority as a duty, the opposite of working for its defeat.

democracy-best.rationale: Wikipedia defines authoritarianism as rejecting political plurality and free competitive elections.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: A communist doctrine, outside general authoritarianism.

direct-votes.rationale: Rule rests on rejecting plurality and free electoral competition, so direct citizen lawmaking contradicts the outlook.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Altemeyer finds hostility to outgroups in followers, but racial policy varies by regime.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Conventionalism includes adherence to traditional norms, such as gender roles.

distribute-by-need.rationale: A distribution principle belongs to economic doctrine, which the sources do not tie to authoritarian rule.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Hobbes puts the subject's duty of obedience to the sovereign ahead of any claim against him, and Altemeyer describes deference to authority as a moral duty.

economic-freedom.rationale: Przeworski stresses prosperity as support for regimes, and many authoritarian states allow markets without political freedom, which rejects the link; the statement is split.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Anti-intellectual themes occur in some followers' attitudes, but the sources do not make this a doctrine.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy view that sometimes appears among followers but is not a defining doctrine.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Wikipedia says authoritarian civil liberties are arbitrarily restricted and repressive power is used against challengers, and Hobbes lets the sovereign decide what peace and defence require.

equal-outcomes.rationale: None of the sources link authoritarian rule to an equality goal; regimes of left and right differ, so adherents split.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Wikipedia notes ethnically based authoritarian rule in some cases, but it is not general.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Regimes protect strategic firms in some cases, but the sources do not make this defining.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Hobbes holds that the sovereign's unaccountable power is compatible with liberty, the opposite of non-domination.

harm-principle.rationale: Wikipedia says civil liberties are arbitrarily restricted and social controls stifle civil society, beyond preventing harm.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Linz describes an executive with ill-defined powers, and Wikipedia ties rule to control of the armed forces by a leader.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: A post-colonial development argument outside what the sources cover.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Wikipedia says authoritarian power is maintained by political repression and armed force against challengers, which contradicts a rule against initiating force.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: A claim about one specific nationalist project, which general authoritarianism neither endorses nor rejects.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Only clerical regimes such as Iran take this line.

limit-population.rationale: Population policy depends on the regime; some have pushed births down and others up, so adherents split.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Wikipedia lists monarchies among authoritarian forms, but many regimes are republican, so adherents split.

national-mission.rationale: Spreading a government form abroad is typical of ideological regimes, whereas Linz notes authoritarian regimes lack an elaborate guiding ideology.

national-rebirth.rationale: Linz says authoritarian regimes lack elaborate, utopian ideology, unlike totalitarian ones; rebirth themes appear in some regimes only.

national-self-determination.rationale: Authoritarian rule is compatible with both national self-determination claims and imperial ones, so adherents split.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental ethics is outside the sources, and authoritarian regimes act both ways toward nature.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Wikipedia describes strong central power with controls over civil society, not a minimal state; Hobbes's sovereign judges almost every area.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Hobbes lets the sovereign decide what doctrines may be taught, which echoes the point, but adherents would not state it that way.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Regimes split between secular and religious schooling.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Wikipedia describes rule by self-appointed leaders and regime-staffed bureaucracies, not chance selection.

one-party-rule.rationale: Linz and Wikipedia identify single-party, military and personal regimes as all authoritarian, and Linz says these regimes lack an elaborate guiding ideology; adherents split.

organic-representation.rationale: Linz notes limited pluralism, which some regimes organize in corporate bodies, but it is not defining.

party-commands-army.rationale: Applies only to single-party states; military regimes do the opposite.

party-controls-media.rationale: Wikipedia lists indoctrination and information control as regime tools, though the statement names the party only.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party discipline matters in single-party regimes but not in military or personal ones that Linz also counts.

people-in-arms.rationale: Wikipedia says power depends on regime control of the armed forces, so an armed citizenry is contrary.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Wikipedia describes rule built on loyalty to a single person, and Altemeyer's authoritarian submission is submission to legitimate authorities.

political-violence-never.rationale: Wikipedia says power is held by repression and armed exclusion of challengers, which contradicts a ban on political violence.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Hobbes holds sovereign rights are indivisible and not to be given away without renouncing sovereignty.

population-transfer.rationale: Followers show hostility to outgroups, but forced transfer is not a general doctrine.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price fixing is used by some authoritarian governments and avoided by others.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Authoritarian regimes cite the poor in some cases, but the sources do not treat this as defining.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Hobbes makes judicature and the sword exclusive rights of the sovereign and indivisible.

production-for-use.rationale: Whether production serves profit or need is an economic matter that varies across authoritarian states.

profit-exploitation.rationale: This is a Marxist claim; some authoritarian regimes embrace capitalist profit and others are communist.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Altemeyer finds hostility to minorities, but segregation law is regime-specific.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Regimes rely on both secular reason and religious authority, as Wikipedia's Iran and Taliban examples contrast with secular states.

recall-officials.rationale: Leaders removable only by free citizen choice contradicts rule where citizens cannot remove leaders by free choice.

restore-past-order.rationale: Wikipedia describes authoritarianism as using strong central power to preserve the status quo, and Altemeyer adds adherence to tradition.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Only some regimes take this line.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Wikipedia describes civil liberties restricted, social controls on civil society, and opposition tolerated little, which covers strike limits.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Linz says authoritarian regimes have mentalities rather than elaborate ideology and often justify themselves by solving problems like underdevelopment.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: National reunification is a goal of some regimes only, and the sources do not treat it as defining.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is a cultural-nationalist policy, not an element of authoritarian rule in the sources.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: A UK housing policy the sources never touch.

right-to-secede.rationale: Hobbes holds subjects cannot change the form of government or break away, and the sovereign's power is indivisible.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The sources contain nothing on rural versus urban life as a moral matter.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Conventionalism and preserving the status quo oppose sacrificing inherited institutions.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Hobbes says the sovereign cannot be punished by subjects for what it does, and Wikipedia describes regimes immune to legal check.

separate-church-state.rationale: Regimes split; Iran and secular states both appear in Wikipedia's account.

separated-powers.rationale: Wikipedia says authoritarian constitutions generally do not limit executive power, and Hobbes holds sovereignty indivisible.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A communist doctrine outside general authoritarianism.

state-as-business.rationale: The statement imagines citizens who can exit; authoritarian rule restricts that and the sources assign it no managerial doctrine.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist doctrine; split for general authoritarianism.

taxation-theft.rationale: Hobbes treats the sovereign's power to tax as part of its rights, so taxation is not theft.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Some regimes expand and others do not.

total-state.rationale: Linz distinguishes authoritarian regimes, with limited pluralism and limited mobilization, from totalitarian ones that direct every area; adherents are split, not strongly agreeing.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist aims occur in some authoritarian economies but are not part of the definition.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Wikipedia lists surveillance and social control as regime tools, so adherents oppose citizens' unreadable communications.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Some authoritarian states unify civil law and others tolerate religious law, so the sources give no single answer.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Wikipedia says leaders can hold office indefinitely and that regimes often lack limits on tenure.

vanguard-party.rationale: A Leninist doctrine outside general authoritarianism.

war-builds-character.rationale: Altemeyer finds aggression toward perceived threats, but this is not a defining doctrine.

workers-councils.rationale: Wikipedia describes power as highly centralized with challengers excluded, which contradicts councils as the basis of power.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Wikipedia and Linz describe exclusion of challengers, limited pluralism and suppression of anti-regime activity as defining features.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Authoritarianism is a form of rule, not a territorial doctrine; regimes make such claims or not as suits them.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Authoritarian regimes both criminalise and tolerate homosexuality; the sources define the system by power, not social policy.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Some regimes enforce religious orthodoxy and others are secular; the label has no religious content.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The doctrine concerns domestic power, and regimes differ on empire; no stated position.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: A religious doctrine outside authoritarianism's scope; regimes differ.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Linz defines authoritarian regimes by limited pluralism and limited political mobilisation, the opposite of direct popular decision-making.

assisted-dying.rationale: No link to the doctrine; regimes vary.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The label covers left, right, religious and military regimes, so adherents are split.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Hobbes grounds sovereignty in the subjects' authorisation rather than God, while many religious autocracies claim divine right; the label as a whole is split.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Authoritarian regimes both ban and mandate religious dress; the sources define the system by control of power, not by this question.

social-market-economy.rationale: Economic order is outside the definition and regimes run state-led, market and mixed economies alike.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Linz and the encyclopedic summary treat control of the armed forces as a main instrument of regime survival, so abolition is contrary to the system.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Authoritarian states have aligned with blocs and stayed non-aligned; foreign alignment is not a defining feature.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Authoritarian regimes include both hereditary monarchies and republics with non-hereditary leaders; the definition concerns concentration of power, not how the ruler is chosen.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Regimes differ: some defy lenders to protect their own control, others accept conditions to stay solvent. The sources define the system by power, not by foreign economic policy.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Authoritarian rulers typically control the press themselves and limit civil liberties, so they do not adopt the claim that formal freedoms are hollow, though left variants would partly agree.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Linz lists ill-defined executive powers among the marks of authoritarian regimes, and Hobbes's sovereign makes law but is not bound by it, so rulers keep room to decide case by case.

racial-franchise.rationale: Ethnically exclusive regimes exist among authoritarian states, but the sources do not make an ethnic franchise a feature of authoritarianism generally.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Altemeyer links authoritarian aggression to hostility toward minorities, but boycotts of a religious minority are not part of the definition and regimes differ.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Authoritarian regimes include both oligarchic and egalitarian ones; the sources define the system by control of power, not by economic distribution.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Authoritarian regimes vary on gay rights; the sources define it by power structure, not social policy.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Authoritarianism rests on control of the armed forces and coercive order, so abolishing police and prisons contradicts it.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Hobbes's account of sovereignty holds that power must be indivisible, and Linz's limited pluralism does not include formal power-sharing among communities.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The sources are silent on social provision; regimes of this type differ on welfare, so no common position is documented.

term-limits.rationale: Managed or absent elections serving regime continuity are a mark of authoritarian rule, so limits on rulers' tenure are disfavoured, though some regimes impose them formally.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Religious office is outside the definition; regimes and adherents differ.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Authoritarian attitudes in Altemeyer's account stress conformity, but regimes of this type differ on family law, so adherents are split.

rent-control.rationale: Authoritarian regimes are defined by control of power, not housing policy; both rent-controlling and market-based regimes exist.

abolish-ip.rationale: Intellectual property is not a theme of the sources; regimes of this kind differ on it.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Linz's authoritarian regimes feature minimal mobilisation, unlike totalitarian ones, but some run youth organisations; adherents are split.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Authoritarian regimes both host and refuse foreign bases; the label does not fix a position.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The label covers regimes of the left and right, so there is no settled view on property income.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Altemeyer reports right-wing authoritarians are hostile to minorities and favour the in-group; other regimes of this kind are not so, hence low confidence.

second-chamber.rationale: Authoritarian states have both unicameral and bicameral legislatures; the sources define the regime by concentrated power, not legislative design.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Authoritarianism concentrates power in the centre and limits political plurality, so decisions resting with local assemblies is the opposite of its model.

family-wage.rationale: An economic and social-policy matter on which the sources record no authoritarian position; adherents differ.

person-over-state.rationale: Altemeyer's account of authoritarian attitudes stresses submission and conformity, and Wikipedia has order and security above individual freedom, so the person is not the state's measure.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Authoritarian regimes include secular, religious and atheist ones; the sources take no stand on human spiritual nature.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Authoritarian regimes span multi-ethnic and nationalist kinds, and the sources define the system by how power is held, not by national identity.

free-public-college.rationale: Authoritarian regimes run both generous and minimal education systems, and the sources define the system by control of power rather than social policy.

pollution-taxes.rationale: The sources define authoritarianism by political control, not economic instruments, and regimes range from heavy polluters to green-minded ones.

future-generations.rationale: Authoritarianism is a form of rule with no stated stance on stewardship, and regimes differ widely in their environmental record.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The label covers regimes of left, right and religious kinds with differing views on gender, so no common position is documented.

capital-controls.rationale: Regimes of this type vary from state-run to market economies, and the sources treat authoritarianism as a form of rule rather than an economic programme.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Hobbes makes the sovereign's monopoly of the sword the basis of order, and Linz-style regimes disarm or control rival armed groups.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Altemeyer's authoritarian submission and the Hobbesian duty of obedience mean soldiers obey lawful orders, including to fight.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Linz's limited pluralism means authoritarian regimes tend to control or co-opt unions, so free collective bargaining is not favoured; regimes vary.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Regimes of all economic kinds exist under the label; the sources define it by power, not economics.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Authoritarianism aims to preserve the regime and its concentrated state power, so dismantling the existing army and bureaucracy is opposed.

sacred-nation.rationale: Altemeyer's authoritarians value national conventions and loyalty, and regimes often invoke the nation; Linz notes this as mentalities rather than a doctrine.

public-service-media.rationale: Wikipedia and Linz describe authoritarian regimes as controlling media and restricting free press, so media independent of government is rejected.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Authoritarian regimes include secular, religious and atheist kinds, and the sources do not tie the label to any view of religion.

farm-price-support.rationale: The label is a form of rule, not an economic programme, and farm policy varies widely across authoritarian regimes.

workers-own-party.rationale: Linz describes limited pluralism and the suppression of independent organisations, so a party outside the regime's control is not welcomed.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Property and gender law are not defined by the label, and right-wing authoritarian attitudes and left-wing regimes differ on it.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Linguistic classification is not an authoritarian issue, and regimes have both promoted and suppressed regional language identities.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Regulation of polluters is not part of the definition; strong-state regimes favour agency or state control but that is an inference, and some regimes favour business.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Authoritarianism puts order above liberty but environmental protection is not a defining priority, so adherents' answers are split.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Union rules are an economic question the definition of authoritarianism does not touch; regimes of both kinds exist.

premarital-sex.rationale: Altemeyer's conventionalism cluster stresses traditional sexual morals and censure of deviation from them.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Welfare design is not part of the definition; regimes differ widely.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Authoritarian regimes include religious, secular and military kinds, so the label carries no scriptural stance.

defend-planned-state.rationale: The label covers left, right and military regimes, so adherents split on defending a planned-economy state.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: A form of rule with no recorded view on borders; regimes take both status-quo and revisionist positions.

simple-living.rationale: The sources treat authoritarianism as a form of rule, with no ideal of simple or self-sufficient living.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Authoritarianism is a form of rule, not a nationalism; regimes of many kinds appeal to the homeland or do not.

close-ties-china.rationale: Foreign alignment varies by regime and the sources take no position.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Authoritarian regimes are defined by power, not economics, so adherents are split on common ownership of resources.

self-ownership.rationale: Linz and Wikipedia describe authoritarianism as placing order and obedience above individual freedom, which cuts against full individual rights.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: The sources describe it as a form of rule with few economic positions, so adherents are split.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The sources describe it as a form of rule with few economic positions, so adherents are split.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Authoritarian regimes span cronyism and strict state control of business; the sources do not settle it.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The label covers secular, religious and military regimes, so adherents are split on denominational politics.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: The label covers regimes of left, right and religious kinds, so adherents are split.

distribution-by-process.rationale: The label covers regimes of left and right; the sources define it by control of power, not by a view of distributive justice.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: The form of rule does not determine a view on racism; Altemeyer's authoritarians are hostile to minorities but regimes of other kinds differ.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Authoritarianism stresses obedience to the ruler; Hobbes holds that subjects cannot judge or depose the sovereign and the sovereign decides which rules bind, and Altemeyer finds authoritarian submission to established authority.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Authoritarianism is a form of rule and has no theory of value; regimes of left and right hold opposite views.

material-over-identity.rationale: Regimes of left and right differ on this; the sources define authoritarianism by control of power, not by the left's priorities.

police-more-powers.rationale: Rule is maintained by control of armed forces and repression of challengers, and Altemeyer links the outlook to submission to and support for force against threats. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

missingStatements.text: Political opposition and independent organisations should be suppressed to preserve order.
missingStatements.rationale: Wikipedia and Linz describe exclusion of challengers, limited pluralism and suppression of anti-regime activity as defining features.

missingStatements.text: Obedience to legitimate authority is a moral duty of citizens.
missingStatements.rationale: Altemeyer's authoritarian submission cluster treats respect for and compliance with authority as a duty, and Hobbes bases the subject's obligation on authorization of the sovereign.

missingStatements.text: Elections should be managed so that the incumbent ruler or ruling group does not lose power.
missingStatements.rationale: Wikipedia describes managed, non-competitive or fraudulent elections and institutions that entrench rule, though some adherents reject elections entirely.
missingStatements.declined: Weak (+1) and disputed among adherents; managed elections are covered loosely by suppress-opposition, one-party-rule and unlimited-reelection.

notes: Hobbes and Altemeyer are theoretical or psychological sources, not a self-described authoritarian movement; few adherents call themselves authoritarian. Left-wing, religious and military authoritarian regimes would answer economic and religious statements differently.
